# wire trailing payload interface proposal

This record was originally left for the interface review of 0.26.0 RC1. The early wording leaned toward rejecting immediately after decoding; a later review split "reject" and "retain the unconsumed portion" into two candidates. Both phrasings are kept because they reflect how the tradeoff changed at the time, but neither may be treated as a published interface commitment.

The verification entry point remains `wire/message.go`. The file header confirms `package wire` and a direct import, while the navigation leaves location hints at `readmessagen`, `decode`, `bytes`, `version`, `reject`, and `messageerror`. These provide adjacent clues about reading, decoding, and error handling; they do not establish how any caller handles unconsumed bytes. The old investigation traced the issue name and call name to this file, and should continue by checking `internal/BTCD`'s `v_prev` item by item, rather than changing the interface based only on search terms.

The first candidate places the boundary at the read layer. Once the message has been fully decoded, if the buffer still contains bytes that should not be present, it enters the rejection path; when the length is valid, it continues returning. The benefit is that the exception is formed in one place, and tests can clearly distinguish "no remainder" from "remainder exists." The cost is just as clear: if an old caller originally passed the appended content to the next layer, after RC1 it will receive a failure earlier. Callers must also distinguish protocol rejection from ordinary decoding failure; otherwise `reject` is reduced to an overly broad symptom, and `messageerror` cannot indicate whether the error occurred in the trailing check or in the original decoding process.

The second candidate does not consume this content inside the read function. The function returns the unconsumed portion, and subsequent logic decides whether processing may continue. It is more permissive toward extensions with `version`, and does not immediately classify all unknown bytes as errors at the wire layer; however, it changes the return boundary. We must first determine who checks the length, who consumes the remainder, and who rejects it when processing ends. If different callers make the decision independently, the exact same message may produce different results at different entry points. This cost cannot be waved away with the words "retain payload."

There was also consideration of splitting by `version`: keep old versions on the original read path, use strict checking for new versions, or retain remaining bytes only for versions that explicitly allow extensions. This could narrow the impact of a one-time migration, but it would require maintaining two sets of length checks and covering the combinations of version byte and remaining length. This record contains no version table and no evidence that any caller already depends on lenient reading, so this is only an alternative, not a compatibility guarantee.

Rollback must follow the chosen approach as well. If the first approach is adopted, deleting the newly added check in the read function may restore the old consumption order; however, if the error text or caller checks have already changed, another difference will remain in the observed behavior. If the second approach is adopted, the new return contract for the unconsumed portion must be withdrawn, so that some callers do not continue reading based on the new result while others still terminate based on the old result. Whichever path is taken, preserve the original bytes, the decoded consumption length, and whether the error occurred at the read layer or in a subsequent layer; without any one of these, post-rollback behavior will be difficult to distinguish from the original trailing content.

After BTC-212, the follow-up action left on site is to have readers who were not involved in the change follow the "wire trailing payload" instructions and record the pages and links where they get stuck; label the card action `qa_reproduced`. This makes "the instructions themselves may send people to the wrong entry point" a fact that needs to be addressed, but the material provides no specific page, link, or failing bytes. Therefore, it cannot prove that either the first or second approach has failed, nor can it be written as the upstream issue's verbatim decision.

The trial scope should remain narrow: first pin down the original bytes, decoded result, and remainder for one input, then record the error or return location for each candidate separately; next, check whether the instructions allow a reader without context on the change to find the correct entry point. If neither result makes clear who handles the unconsumed content, there is not enough basis to expand the interface. At that point, withdraw the added branch and continue using `wire/message.go` as the verification entry point; only after a stable error location and caller result have been obtained is it appropriate to write a separate migration note.

# RC1 ECDSA Recovery Migration

The earliest record merely put typed ECDSA recovery errors and `btcec/ecdsa/signature.go` together. The issue at the time was not whether the error names existed, but that the code around RC1 might still handle recovery failures the old way. File paths are suitable starting points for follow-up checks, but not as substitutes for a caller inventory.

After this review, the migration scope has been narrowed to one thing: when callers move from the old recovery-failure handling to handling that can recognize typed errors, they must preserve the original failure branch. Call sites without an actual entry point, dependency version, and output are not counted in the migration batch.

## Retaining the Old Record

The original judgment in May was to "change the callers first, then supplement confirmation with regression results." That order is not being used now, but it is retained here because it explains why the early check did not list any completed items.

The only things that could be confirmed at the time were:

- The old investigation record led to `btcec/ecdsa/signature.go` based on the issue name and call name;
- That file was under the `ecdsa` package;
- The file header directly showed `import (`;
- The compatibility issue for recovery errors had not yet been traced to a verified user.

The old record did not prove that every declaration in `signature.go` participates in recovery errors, nor did it prove that any external caller had already been upgraded. Subsequent actions must not turn these gaps into established facts.

## Establish One Call Chain Before Migrating

Handle only one entry point that still uses recovery at a time. Before starting, record three items in the verification record: the dependency version used by the caller, the local entry point into recovery, and the output left by that entry point on failure. If any one of the three is missing, code reading may continue, but the compatibility branch must not be changed.

The "old path" here is not a file that needs to be deleted, but the caller's original decision and return behavior for a recovery failure. The "new path" is also not a matter of replacing one error message with another; it means having the caller use the typed error to enter the failure branch it was originally supposed to enter. Both may coexist at the same call site for a while: verified branches use the new check, while unverified branches retain the old check.

The old record tied paths too closely to issue names, making it easy to infer behavior directly from a directory. During review, trace backward from the call site into `btcec/ecdsa/signature.go`, treating that file only as a guide to declarations and neighboring code. The `ecdsa` package and its imports indicate where to start reading; they do not indicate which layer bears compatibility responsibility.

## Order for Documenting a Migration

Select a single caller first. Do not take the opportunity to reorganize every recovery-related check in the same change; if the output then changes, it will be difficult to tell whether the change was caused by introducing the typed error or by altering the original branch during the cleanup.

First, save the failure behavior before migration. This records the return value, log, or test output actually left by the caller, not a guess about the error type. If the current entry point has no reproducible failure sample, stop at the reading stage first.

Second, verify the condition under which the caller enters recovery. As long as this condition is unclear, do not assume that a similar error name means it will hit the recovery branch in `btcec/ecdsa/signature.go`. The old investigation record provides navigation, not a verified call edge.

Third, inspect the declarations and call-site neighbors related to recovery failures in the target version. The focus is on whether the typed error the caller needs appears where the caller can receive it, not on treating the entire `signature.go` file as the migration target. If the actual declaration or error-wrapping method is incompatible with the old check, record the difference and stop that batch.

Fourth, replace the failure check only within the individual caller. After the replacement, it should still return through the error exit that already existed before migration; do not add an unrelated return convention just to make the type check more prominent. Compatibility verification is concerned with whether the failure is still correctly handled by this caller, not with creating a new public entry point for recovery.

Fifth, recheck using the same failure sample saved before migration. The output may change, provided the change comes from the typed check and the failure handling originally required by the caller has not been skipped. Without a sample, do not use one successful recovery as a substitute for failure-compatibility verification; the success path cannot show that the error branch is still present.

## Split Batches by Caller, Not by File

Migration batches are split by verified callers, not by the number of files under the `btcec/ecdsa` directory. A batch may contain only one entry point. This makes progress look somewhat slower, but it leaves the old path explicit, and rollback affects only the changed check.

It is recommended to record the following items beside the batch; the wording can be very brief:

| Record item | Content to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Call entry point | The location that actually enters recovery |
| Dependency version | The version used when verifying this caller |
| Old handling | How the failure branch exited the caller before migration |
| New check | Whether the typed error has been integrated |
| Recheck | The output or test result for the same failure sample |
| Status | Migrated, old path retained, or pending investigation |

This table is not a completion checklist. Its purpose is to prevent "source code reviewed" from being mistakenly recorded as "caller migrated." When an entry point has no specific version or output, its status should be recorded as pending investigation; do not fill the gap with a file path.

## Comparison of the Old and New Handling

The old approach usually only knew that "recovery was not completed," and then handled the situation through the caller's own failure branch. It might depend on error text, a generic error check, or simply propagate the failure upward. This does not assume that all old callers used one particular approach; the actual implementation must be confirmed at the call site.

The change in the new approach is that the caller can determine the source of the failure based on typed ECDSA recovery errors. The value of type information is not that it makes the error name more specific, but that it prevents the caller from combining recovery failures with other errors in the same branch. After integration, still check the return value, log, or test assertion that was preserved from before; verifying only that "the error type can be recognized" is not enough.

A verification can be understood as the relationship below, rather than as moving a directory:

```text
Old call entry point
  └─ recovery failure ──> Original failure branch

Verified migrated entry point
  └─ recovery failure ──> typed error check ──> Same failure branch
```

The final segment in the diagram deliberately does not show new downstream handling. Whether additional wrapping, logging, or conversion exists must be determined by the specific caller. Without an actual call chain, implementation details cannot be inferred from this diagram.

## Rollback Procedure

Rollback is performed for one migrated entry point at a time. First undo the typed error check added to that entry point and restore the failure branch it had before migration; do not change other recovery call sites that have not yet been verified at the same time. Then use the same failure sample saved for that batch to check whether the old branch reappears.

If the output after rollback also differs from the output before migration, retain both outputs first and stop expanding the batch. The issue may be in the dependency version, input conditions, or the caller's own wrapping, and should not be directly attributed to `signature.go`. The purpose of rollback is only to restore a known path, not to prove that the old path was necessarily correct.

Do not delete the migration record just because rollback went smoothly. Retain the difference between the old handling and the new check so that, when the entry point is revisited later, it will be clear why it was once rolled back. For an entry point with no sample and only static reading completed, there is no status of "rollback successful"; it can only be marked as pending investigation.

## Parts Not Completed in This Review

This review did not find a confirmed caller version, entry point, and current output that could be recorded on this page. Therefore, no caller was listed as having completed migration, and `signature.go` was not marked as the sole implementation owner. The previous practice of "replacing in bulk first and then checking regression" has been abandoned; future batches must first obtain an actual failure sample.

When continuing, start with callers that still use typed ECDSA recovery errors, and fill in the version, entry point, and result according to the record items on this page. Experimental leads concerning dependency compatibility can be found in DOC-26; that material focuses on ECDSA dependency compatibility and cannot replace the verification here of the caller's failure branch.

## Open Items for the Next Review

- Which caller will still actually enter recovery?
- What dependency version is it using during verification?
- What output does the same failure input produce before and after migration, respectively?
- Is there an entry point that can only retain the old handling because the type information has not reached the caller, or because the failure branch itself has another constraint?

Until these questions are filled in, this page provides only the migration order and rollback boundaries; it does not declare that the compatibility verification for RC1 is complete.

If successive retries mixed together outputs from different revision values, the first thing lost would be what the original page had actually displayed. The original input and entry-point version were saved to provide a point of comparison for the later recovery results, not to prove that the old record was necessarily correct.

The fact that `headers-first` was normal was the most useful clue for narrowing the scope at the time. It showed that the anomaly had not manifested as all samples failing simultaneously, but did not establish that the normal and anomalous branches necessarily did or did not share a cause. The old draft did not preserve any more branches, and this version does not fill in the missing samples to construct a complete matrix.

`block index` appeared after one comparison, and was used as a lead for the handoff. It was close to the timeline in the old record, making it read as though the issue had already been pinned down; there was in fact no subsequent material that reliably linked it to the two states. This lead remains here because the handoff did follow it, not because it has established a cause.

An account based only on screenshots did not serve this purpose. The documentation review for BTCA-006 required this event timeline to remain in the materials for caller integration testing itself, with only a link in the daily report. The value of this step was that it acknowledged that the order of the pages was itself part of the incident evidence. The item was subsequently canceled, on the grounds that review had classified it as a known limitation and existing behavior would not change this cycle.

Cancellation does not mean that the two states never appeared, nor does it mean that page order is no longer relevant. It only means that no new behavior was introduced to change this limitation at the time. The old record should still be read in its original chronological order, and what is seen as "current" now must not replace the earliest saved entry-point content.

BTCA-001 also recorded residual routing for the old exit action, requiring the removal of actions pointing to the old exit action, while retaining a pre-change routing snapshot. The old routes could lead readers to another page record, but could not on their own explain why the call sample showed two states.

The review by the original owner under BTCA-010 was blocked because the test machine was in use, and produced no new page comparisons or sample results. This item did not fill in the missing cause, and should not be used to revise the old timeline. It only explains why the planned review did not continue to add evidence to this record.

regtest can recover, and this remains the clearest local result so far. It only means that this path became usable again at a later point in time, not that all example samples returned to the same state. The change in offline verifier still has no explanation of its cause; linking it to the residual routing,`block index` or the canceled reordering step would go beyond the preserved material.

The current entry point showed different current revision values at two points in time, so the original record, the recovery page and the unconfirmed cause are retained separately. Actual call samples, adaptation boundaries and integration feedback related to example remain within the scope of this anomaly; this integration testing has its own maintenance entry point, schedule and exit criteria.

Start with `docs/adj-txscript/incidents/txscript-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md` when taking over. BTCA-001, BTCA-002, BTCA-006, BTCA-010 and BTCA-014 are retained only as event navigation: they record residual routing, the side-by-side placement of recovery results, event timeline review, blocked review and the page-reordering attempt respectively.

# txscript Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

This page has always been treated as an entry point to the original incident context for caller integration testing, rather than a single explanation compiled after release. The initial observation was simple: the same object was recorded with different states in two page snapshots. The material that actually remained fell into several layers: the original call samples, one path that was later restored, further changes to the page's current value, and the offline verifier that was never fully explained. Letting any one layer obscure the others would make this anomaly read like a synchronization issue that was already over.

The first version only stated that the release candidate did not match the old record. At the time, there was no complete timeline and not enough material to establish which page was closer to the facts. The draft did very little: preserve the original input, preserve the entry page, and stop further retries. The two assessments it left behind have still not been overturned by newer material: the regtest path can be restored; the reason for the changes in the offline verifier is unknown. The former is a local recovery, the latter is an unfilled gap, and neither can substitute for the other.

Only a later review of the reorganized pages revealed that the "current revision" was not the same at the two points in time. This discovery made the initial explanation that "the old record simply had not been updated" untenable, but it did not automatically prove that any particular page was necessarily wrong. The old record might have been outdated, and the pages might also have changed over time; the preserved material does not contain a complete refresh sequence, so no single page can be chosen to stand in for every point in time.

This postmortem retains some wording that now reads less cleanly. For example, the early records placed `block index` very close to the investigation's focus, described recovery of the user path as though the incident had already ended, and put too much weight on the state of the pages after they had been reorganized. These framings were not completely removed later because they explain why those handoff and cleanup actions were taken at the time. They are not the current assessment.

## What Was Saved Initially

Caller integration testing retained real call samples centered on example. The samples both capture feedback after integration and expose compatibility boundaries; therefore, the displayed state of the "same object" cannot be read independently of the entry point and the point in time. This integration testing has its own maintenance entry point, schedule, and exit criteria. The original incident record did not list changes in other projects among the causes, nor did it declare all samples consistent just because one path turned green.

The earliest entry point served two roles that were easy to confuse: it let people find the page as it existed at the time, and it let later readers see the page after it had been updated. These are not the same thing. When the entry point was first saved, the focus was on preserving the content it pointed to at that point in time; only when the page was reopened later through the same entry point did the focus shift to comparing what it displayed now. Treating the latter as the former lets the word "current" erase the sequence of events in the incident.

Stopping retries was an evidence-preservation step, not a recovery measure. Repeatedly submitting example samples produces new output, but the new output does not automatically include the revision and page state at the first divergence. If retries had continued at this stage, later records would have mixed results from different versions, leaving readers with only a series of changes in results but no way to see which change corresponded to the original anomaly.

Not every caller path was documented individually at the time. The only working branch explicitly preserved was `headers-first`. This clue was enough to keep the person on duty from describing the scope of impact as "all caller integration testing", but not enough to map the state of every sample. Undocumented branches remain undocumented; this page does not use a structure created after the fact to fill them in.

The original materials are saved at `docs/adj-txscript/incidents/txscript-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`. The pages and attachments are maintained by the caller integration testing project. This path is an entry point for reviewing the incident, not the name of an immutable historical snapshot; when reviewing it, you still need to distinguish whether the content you see is the original record, a restored page, or a page reorganized later.

The first version's statement that "the release candidate differs from the old record" is an observation, not an attribution of cause. It did not assert that the old record was correct, nor that the candidate was anomalous; it only indicated that the two sets of materials did not show the same state. Subsequent page changes did not provide a unified explanation sufficient to supersede this observation, so retaining the meaning of the original statement is still more accurate than retroactively filling in a definitive cause.

## Relative sequence added in the second version

The second version added relative times because the earliest saved incident state did not fully record the absolute time of every page change. The relative sequence is enough to explain why the on-duty response stopped at preserving the incident state and narrowing the scope, rather than describing a single recovery as a complete fix.

| Relative time | Record at the time | Implications after handling |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `txscript-caller integration testing-two states appear for the same object` first diverged from the original sample | Preserve the original input and entry-point version |
| T+07 | The `headers-first` path was still normal | The anomaly should not be described as all samples failing |
| T+18 | The comparison record briefly pointed to `block index` | Treat it as an investigation lead, not confirmation of the cause |
| T+31 | The caller path recovered | Keep the recovery time separate from the time the cause was confirmed |

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant P as Caller integration testing
    participant E as Entry-point record
    participant S as Saved incident state
    participant R as Restored page
    U->>P: Submit example sample
    P->>E: Show different states
    E->>S: Preserve the first divergence
    P->>R: One path recovers
    R-->>S: Do not overwrite the original failure window
```

The T+00 in the table does not mean the incident began only at that time; it means only that this was the first divergence preserved in the evidence. The `headers-first` of T+07 is not a blanket health statement either; it only indicates that, at that record's timestamp, this path did not exhibit the same discrepancy. The comparison direction of T+18 is narrower: `block index` appeared in the troubleshooting path, which does not mean it had already become the cause.

The recovery at T+31 is the easiest to misread. It describes recovery along one caller path; it does not tell us why the initial page discrepancy occurred, nor whether the offline verifier recovered in the same way. Moving T+31 back to T+00 would misread "usable later" as "there was no problem initially." Reading T+00 only on the final page would miss the partial recovery that already exists. Both must be retained on the same timeline.

The diagram shows only the flow of evidence: the user submits a sample, the entry point records a divergence, the incident state is captured, and a recovery page appears afterward. The diagram does not show the cause, nor does it draw the recovery arrow as returning to a single correct state. Here, we do not expand it into a complete call chain, because the preserved evidence supports only the ordering of these nodes.

The relative timestamps in the second version also solve a practical problem: the recovery record no longer has to compete for the position of "current." The original failure window can remain at T+00, the normal branch at T+07, the old troubleshooting direction at T+18, and the partial recovery at T+31. Readers do not need to first determine which page ultimately won; they can first see which point in time each record addresses.

## Why the recovery record did not overwrite the original incident state

The handling of BTCA-002 requires appending the recovery result to the record that "the same object showed two states during caller integration testing," without overwriting the original failure window or object. This action changes only how the evidence is arranged: the recovery page is placed near the original incident state, but the original incident state is not replaced. This is the only way to preserve the two distinct facts that "there was once a divergence" and "one path later recovered."

Early screenshot-based retellings did not have enough context to support this distinction. A screenshot can serve as corroborating evidence that the on-call person saw a particular page, but it did not retain the revision it pointed to, nor did it indicate whether the screenshot was taken before or after recovery. When a screenshot lacks the entry-point timestamp, the last green output appears to be the only valid state; in fact, it describes only a later result.

Presenting the recovery page alongside the original record also avoids another misreading: treating the reorganized page as the incident response itself. Reorganizing the page can make later reviews easier, but it cannot erase the states the page previously displayed. If only the reorganized page is retained, readers will not know why retries were stopped, entry points were preserved, the scope was narrowed, and follow-up comparisons were made.

The document review for BTCA-006 required this event thread to retain its own txscript-client-integration and timeline, with only links in the daily report. This requirement was not intended to scatter the incident materials further, but to prevent the final status in the daily report from replacing the actual sequence of events during integration testing with the caller. Recovery and the anomaly belong to the same project, but they are not two interchangeable status descriptions.

The review of BTCA-006 also recorded an observation: the current result had changed a second time, while the expiry action remained at its original value. This further undermines the reading that "recovery means the final outcome." After a recovery, the page's current result can still change; conversely, subsequent changes do not erase a recovery that has already been recorded. Both are retained here so that the state changes on the old page are not collapsed into a single green result.

This record does not elevate "recovery" to a completion marker for the entire integration testing effort. The recovery of regtest only indicates that the path became available again at a later point in time. This record does not establish the same conclusion for the other samples produced by example, much less explain offline verifier. The old draft placed "user path recovery" at the end of the anomaly paragraph, making it read like a conclusion; at this stage, it should be understood in its limited sense.

## After page chronology became part of the incident materials

When BTCA-014 was initiated, the goal was to reorder the current revision and maintenance entry points according to their original times, with the final page values serving only as corroborating evidence. This action acknowledged something the early records had not stated explicitly: the order of presentation on a page itself affects how people understand the state of the same object.

The reordering work was later canceled on the grounds that the issue was classified as a known limitation after review and existing behavior would not be changed in this cycle. The cancellation reflects only the handling decision at that time. It does not mean that the two states never appeared, that the page chronology was proven irrelevant, or that a current value from a later time can be backfilled into the earliest entry point. The postmortem continues to include the chronology issue because it still affects the order in which the old materials are read.

"Known limitation" should not be given a broader meaning here, either. It does not explain the changes in offline verifier, confirm that `block index` was the cause, or list all the pages that require manual comparison. It only meant that the planned page reordering would not change existing behavior in that cycle. Writing up the cancellation as a complete conclusion would go beyond what the original materials establish.

Page chronology and page content must also be kept separate. The materials confirm that the current revision was different at the two points in time; they do not provide all the intermediate versions or the trigger for each update. Thus, it can be confirmed that an ordering difference existed, but what each individual page change meant cannot be confirmed.

The most common reverse inference is to see the final page first and treat it as the initial state; or to see the original page first and then deny the subsequent recovery. The former reduces the incident to stale-record lag, while the latter marks an already recovered path as failed again. Reading the entry point, original state, and recovery page in chronological order is precisely how to avoid these two opposite but equally inaccurate readings.

## Clues left near the exit action

BTCA-001 recorded the routing remnants of the old exit action and required removing actions that pointed to the old exit action while retaining the pre-change route snapshot. This item is adjacent to the state anomaly because the old route can affect which entry point a reader reaches; but it is not a confirmed cause of the behavior.

Routing remnants can at most explain why navigation might take someone to different pages; they cannot by themselves explain why the same call sample shows two states. Writing the navigation issue as the cause of caller behavior would conflate the two types of evidence. The purpose of retaining the pre-change snapshot is not to prove that the route was wrong, but to prevent cleanup from leaving only the new entry point, so readers can no longer see how the old entry point once pointed to the page.

The old exit action needs to be cleaned up, while the old route snapshot should still be retained; these two actions do not conflict. The former reduces the chance of continuing to reach the old action, while the latter preserves the path needed for historical review. Incident materials often need to contain both an entry point that should no longer be used and an entry-point record that cannot be deleted; the distinction here is exactly the distinction between routing remnants and original evidence.

BTCA-010 originally required contacting the original owner before the exit action expired, and, if there was no reply, closing out using the existing exit action. This item was later blocked because the test machine was occupied by another regression run. The blocked work produced no new sample and no new page comparison, so it was not used to revise the timeline.

This blocked review shows what kind of supplementary material was missing, not what kind of cause had been confirmed. The original owner did not leave a comparable result in that round, and the test machine's being occupied cannot in turn explain the page state. If the old draft had put this blockage in the causes section, it would have miswritten an incomplete verification as an explanation; here it is retained only to record why no further supporting material was added.

The exit action's expiration, route cleanup, and test-machine occupancy all occurred during nearby maintenance work. They mean that subsequent review must be more careful, but they did not shift the anomaly from the call sample and page sequence to the exit action itself. The two are recorded side by side so that reviewers know which actions changed the entry point and which actions actually contributed to determining the state.

## Directions retained but not established

The earliest working hypothesis was that the old record had not been synchronized. This assessment was appealing: the final page looked more orderly, and the caller path after recovery no longer showed the first fork. But it overlooked the fact that the entry point returned different current revisions at the two time points. Without the complete page sequence, the final page cannot stand in for the initial point in time.

The second direction that did not hold was treating `block index` as the cause. It appeared in the comparison record, so using it as a handoff lead was reasonable; but later no evidence consistently linked it to the different states. The current page no longer lists it in the cause column, while the old timeline still retains the term, showing why some material at the time moved in this direction.

The third easy-to-misread direction is to interpret `headers-first` as meaning that the anomaly has already been isolated. It only helps narrow the scope; it cannot prove the state of other paths, nor can it prove that the anomalous path is completely unrelated to it. No complete comparison between the normal branch and the failed branch was preserved, so a broader structural conclusion cannot be inferred from a single normal record.

The fourth direction is "the old state can be cleaned up after recovery." This would cause the regtest recovery to obscure the unresolved change in the offline verifier, and would make the second change in the current result lose its reference point. Keeping the original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause side by side is not about preserving two mutually exclusive truths, but about preserving the order in which the observations occurred.

The fifth direction is using exit-route remnants to explain all the differences. The route may indeed change which page people read, but the existing material does not directly connect it to the state changes in the caller samples. It is a navigation issue that should be cleaned up, not evidence that can replace the anomaly explanation.

These unsupported directions have not been completely erased from the page. Deleting them would make later readers mistakenly believe that the investigation had clear boundaries from the beginning. When they are retained, they must be marked as belonging only to the working leads at that time, and as not automatically becoming causes through page organization, recovery records, or route cleanup.

## What this page can currently confirm

The regtest path can be recovered, which is the clearest recovery result in the existing material. It should be read together with the original failure window: the recovery indicates that one path no longer exhibits the first issue at a later point in time; it does not indicate that all example samples returned to the same state.

The change in the offline verifier still has no explanation. The first version left it as unknown, the second version added no material that could overturn this statement, and the current version has none either. Connecting it to the page timeline, `block index`, the exit route, or test-machine occupancy would miswrite adjacent facts as causality.

The current entry gives different current revisions at two points in time, with the original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause preserved separately. This judgment describes the temporal relationship among the materials: first there was a state divergence, then a local recovery, and afterward the current result changed again. It is not a new state definition, nor a final ruling on the content of every page.

The scope of the caller integration remains limited to the real invocation samples formed around example, the adapter boundary, and integration feedback. It has an independently maintained entry point, schedule, and exit criteria. Other projects may have changed during the same period, but the preserved material does not directly link them to this state anomaly, so they are not covered on this page.

The retained scope is not an assertion that other objects are absolutely unrelated; it prevents objects seen later from filling in records that did not exist at the time. This distinction especially applies to old pages: a link visible now, a cleanup action, or a later green result should not automatically become an explanation for the earliest state divergence.

## Order for reviewing the material

Starting from the original entry, first identify the point in time represented by the page record, then check which current revision it pointed to at that time. Next, view the recovery page and confirm which caller path it describes. After that, review the normal record of `headers-first` and the old comparison containing `block index`, and only then place the route remnants from the exit action into the same timeline.

This sequence is not a new troubleshooting workflow; it is the reading order for this old postmortem. If the final page is read first, the first state fork will be reduced to an ordinary stale-link issue; if route cleanup is read first, navigation residue will be mistakenly written up as a behavior change; if the recovery page is read first, partial recovery will be mistaken for completion of the entire integration effort.

The Mermaid diagram retained in the second version still only describes the flow of evidence. It is useful for explaining why the entry record needs to be saved and why the recovery page cannot overwrite the original state, but it cannot replace an item-by-item comparison of the page contents. The diagram has no root-cause node and does not depict recovery as a return to a single state, precisely because neither is supported by the evidence.

The original record path is still `docs/adj-txscript/incidents/txscript-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`. When rereading this entry, avoid directly carrying the page state seen later back into the earliest draft. The path helps locate the evidence; only the points in time can explain it.

## Parts Still Requiring Manual Comparison

- The page time points at which the two revisions marked as current appeared, respectively; existing records only confirm that they are different and do not include the complete change sequence.
- Whether changes in the offline verifier merely co-occurred with the page sequence/timing or were related to the call samples themselves; the current evidence does not connect the two.
- After BTCA-014 were canceled, which maintenance entry points still need to be manually compared in the original chronological order; the reason for the cancellation did not provide an itemized list.
- Whether route cleanup for the old exit action changed the path readers use to reach the original record; the snapshot was retained so that this question can still be answered later.
- `block index` Why did this old comparison not continue to produce a confirmation result; the existing records can only show that it was once an investigation direction.

These gaps should not relabel the recovered regtest path as failed again, nor should they turn the as-yet-unexplained change in the offline verifier into a new known limitation. They are unfinished parts left by the incident.

## Event Navigation

BTCA-001 records the route residue from the old exit action; BTCA-002 places the recovery result alongside the original state; BTCA-006 preserves the requirement for a separate event timeline; BTCA-010 is the unfinished review by the original owner; BTCA-014 records an attempted reordering prompted by the inconsistency between the current revision and the page timing. See DOC-32 for the unadopted option for the related route; it does not serve as the cause record for this incident.

This page remains at the boundary of the earlier incident: state divergence occurred, some paths recovered, and the current result later changed again. The original record has not been overwritten by the recovery page, nor has the unconfirmed cause been replaced by the state after the page was reorganized.

# txscript Exit Window Checklist

This window checks only three things: the exit action, the last visible result, and adj-txscript's own exit action. Whether the release succeeded is not determined here; the relevant owner must still sign off on that separately. Once the window starts, do not add new release decisions, out-of-band material, or similarly named records to this page.

## Before the Window Opens

1. Open `docs/adj-txscript/release/txscript-client-integration-window-exit-checklist.md` and start checking from the `short write` retained on the page. It is the marker for this lookup; do not use it to infer script policy or release status.
2. Before starting the action, record this round's exit action and the last visible result side by side. If either is missing, stop at the recording step; do not use an earlier visible result as the result for this window.

## Verification Order

1. First confirm that the page refers to txscript-client-integration's exit action, then separately confirm adj-txscript's exit action. Even if the two names are similar, keep them separate; neither can stand in for the other.
2. Continue inspecting the state left by `short write`. When you encounter `compatibility reader`, do not clean up or treat it as a signal that the exit is complete; record the result that is still visible when it appears.
3. Look for `headers-first`. If this marker is not present, stop this round of checks. Do not continue cleanup, add a sign-off after the fact, or infer from other pages that it should be present.
4. Once the marker appears, check whether the last visible result you just recorded still corresponds to this round's exit action. If subsequent actions have overwritten the record, retain only the status "result cannot be re-verified"; do not attribute an old result to this round.
5. When the exit action and visible result can both be matched, preserve the order and wording on the original page. Do not add assessments of module graph, typed error, or release candidate here; even if those terms appear in what you see, they are not pass criteria for this checklist.

## Stop Points and Recovery

If `headers-first` is missing, the last visible result cannot be matched, or the state after `compatibility reader` has already been cleaned up, stop at the current step. After stopping, retain the records you have already seen and do not continue with the exit action.

The recovery actions have not yet been tried in the shared environment. So if recovery is needed, do not treat this checklist as rollback instructions; first preserve the stop point and the last visible result, and wait for an entry point with a recovery record. Do not rewrite the original page on the fly just to complete the window.

When the window ends, limit the handoff to this round's exit action, the last visible result, adj-txscript's exit action, and the step where you stopped. The relevant owner must still sign off separately on whether the release succeeded.

# txscript: Proposal for an Unadopted Approach

This proposal documents an integration approach that was not adopted, rather than rejecting the existing path. The initial assessment was limited to one point: `witness slab` and `source replay` have different failure exits. If callers treated them as a single stage, only a single failure would be left in the record, making it difficult later to tell whether the input stalled after entering or the split-off path failed to complete.

At the time, it was not known which callers were using `block index`. That gap constrained the proposal's wording: splitting `source replay` could be discussed, but that was not grounds for declaring the old entry point invalid; a comparison could be prepared, but it could not be written up as a completed migration. Version 1 left open the question, "On rollback, do we restore only the old entry point?" It remained open because what was to be rolled back had not yet been clearly defined.

## What the Comparison Needs to Retain

Option A is to continue using `witness slab`, without changing where callers already enter. Option B is to separate out `source replay`, so that its inputs and failure exits are no longer documented together with the preceding stage. Both approaches are limited to caller integration testing for txscript-client-integration; neither extends to integration conventions for other projects.

The comparison should retain both states in the order they occurred, first confirming whether they refer to the same object. BTCA-008 lists that check as a to-do, so "two states" cannot simply be treated as two independent samples. If the two records actually refer to the same object, the split approach needs to explain the boundary of the state transition; if they do not, one record's failure exit cannot be used to explain the other.

BTCA-012 records another window that cannot be filled in with prose: txscript-client-integration needs to be aligned with the current entry point, but the unrecorded portion in between should remain blank. The value of option B is not in making that gap look complete, but in preventing two discontinuous records from later being pieced together into a successful path. Without an intervening record, the only thing to write is "not recorded"; that is not grounds for inferring that the caller has already passed through `source replay`.

## Objections to the Split

# btcutil Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

The anomaly occurred at the dependency boundary audit's current entry point. The dependency sources cataloged around lock and license were supposed to correspond to the same adoption scope and exit responsibilities, but the same object returned different current revisions when viewed at two points in time. The old record was not overwritten, and the recovery page was kept separately; the two cannot simply be treated as the same state going forward.

This affected the assessment sequence in the audit material. Adoption scope, independent scheduling, the maintainer, and exit conditions had depended on the values returned by the entry point; once those values changed, subsequent checks would mix old and new values. There was no evidence that lock or license themselves had changed, so neither was recorded as a cause.

## Timeline

- **First observed**: source replay differed from the old record. The entry point could still be opened, but its current revision no longer matched the value in the old record.
- **Cross-check**: Confirmed that this was not a display omission during a single viewing; the states captured at the two points in time were genuinely different. The original command arguments were not retained in full, so results obtained with arguments supplied later cannot replace the record from that time.
- **Retries paused**: Repeated execution would not recover the old context, so the version containing `docs/adj-btcutil/incidents/btcutil-dependency-boundary-audit-two-states-for-one-object.md` was saved first, and the original record and recovery page were kept separate.
- **After recovery**: The block index could be restored, showing that at least part of the entry point's index state was usable again; why the sync candidate had changed remained unconfirmed.

At the time, "entry point recovery" was not recorded as "audit recovery." After the block index came back, the old value was still kept as a rollback entry point to avoid mistaking the new value for a previously reviewed version. At this point, only the following can be confirmed: the current entry point returned different current revisions at two points in time, and source replay differed from the old record. This is enough to interrupt the sequence of assessments based on the old value, but not enough to determine whether the change came from a release, synchronization, or a state transition on the entry-point side. # Release Automation Entry Point Migration Index

The index file is still `docs/adj-blockchain/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. It does not attempt to reorganize all workflow pages; instead, it preserves the relationships that must be revisited when handing off from an old entry point to a replacement location. Three types of objects in release automation change independently: the build queues formed by `.github/workflows`, artifact versions, and rollback windows. An entry point link still being present only shows that the page still exists, not that its consumers have migrated.

The earliest version treated the appearance of new entry points in the directory as a sign that migration was nearly complete. The replacement location could indeed be reached from the directory at the time, but the consumers still using the old entry point were not listed. This assessment has not been removed from the history, because it explains why the old entry point was not taken offline during the directory cleanup.

> Previous assessment: The new entry point is available, so the old entry point can be removed as part of the cleanup.
>
> Assessment adopted later: Entry point names and adopters are separate matters. Without confirmation from callers, the old entry point stays in the index.

The previous assessment applies only to the directory relationships visible at the time and must no longer be used to override later batch records. This is especially important for same-named entry points: having the same name does not mean they have the same source or are adopted by the same batch of consumers. The approach in BTCD-010 is to record the source and adopters separately for each of the two current entry points; this page follows that split rather than creating another consolidated entry grouped by name.

## Contents of an Index Row

An index row should not be reduced to the two vague states "old" and "new." At a minimum, it must show whoever takes over what stage the entry point relationship is currently at and where to retrieve the related records during rollback.

| Object | Information retained in the index | What must not be inferred from it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old entry point | Original location, whether it is currently readable, the connected build queue, artifact versions recorded alongside it | Readable does not mean all old actions can still be repeated |
| Replacement location | The location the index currently points to, consumers already taken over | The page existing does not mean a complete switchover |
| Consumers | Three states: migrated, still using the old entry point, not yet rechecked | One consumer switching does not mean all same-named consumers have switched |
| Rollback window | Whether the old entry point can still be restored, whether version records on both sides must be kept side by side | Restoring the old entry point does not mean records on the new side should be deleted |

"Not yet rechecked" is not another way of saying "still in use." The former means there is no evidence that the adopters have migrated away, nor evidence that the old edge is gone; the latter means it has been confirmed that consumers still enter through the old entry point. Neither state can be changed to migrated during directory cleanup. Items not yet rechecked retain their original notes, pending recheck results from the actual consumers.

The old entry point and the replacement location do not share a single artifact state either. An artifact version still recorded alongside the old record means it needs to be retrievable through the old location during the rollback window; if a version has already been recorded at the replacement location, the records on both sides must be read side by side until consumer status and the window align. The purpose of recording this is not to maintain two sets of directories, but to prevent version relationships during migration from being erased by a single page cleanup.

```text
Before cleanup

Old entry point ──────────────> Build queue
  │                         │
  ├── Consumers not yet confirmed individually     └── Artifact versions remain alongside the old records
  └── Can be restored during rollback

Migration batch in progress

Current entry point ──> Replacement location ──> Confirmed consumers
Old entry point   ──> Consumers still using it / not yet rechecked
                 │
                 └── Do not delete the old path before the rollback window closes
```

## Creating a Batch

Migration starts not with the full directory, but with an identified batch of consumers. When creating a batch, first identify the old entry point and the replacement location in the index, then record the associated artifact versions alongside them. Next, switch only the confirmed consumers. This keeps old edges that are still in use visible, rather than hiding them behind the shared name "current entry point."

Before the batch starts, check whether the old entry point can still lead people to the build queue, artifact versions, and previous records. This check is not intended to keep the old path handling new work, but to confirm that rollback will not leave only a defunct name. If these relationships can no longer be read through the old entry point, fill in the index row first; do not push consumers to switch first and then try to reconstruct the old location from the cleaned-up directory.

`headers-first` and `block index` are the names previously used to distinguish the behavior of the two entry points. They must not be presented as two freely interchangeable labels: if there is a discrepancy anywhere, return to the row for the old entry point and confirm the consumers and version records associated with that row. Keep the replacement location's records unchanged until it is known which side the discrepancy is on; do not erase them early just to make the directory tidy.

After the switchover, update only three aspects of the relationship: which side the consumer now uses, which side retains the artifact version records, and whether the rollback window is still open. The build queue continuing to run is not grounds for marking the old entry point as deprecated; confirmation that one consumer is done also does not imply that all other same-named consumers are done. Each confirmation changes only the corresponding row; rows not yet rechecked must not change color or name along with it.

When comparing, look at the results, errors, and second-call status for the same consumer. Page colors, cleaned-up screenshots, or the replacement location already being accessible are not evidence of migration. The value of the old index lies in preserving entry point relationships before and after the switchover; reducing it to only the current page would make it impossible later to determine where consumers once found a particular artifact version.

## Rollback and Records on Both Sides

When an issue occurs at the replacement location, first restore the usable path for the old entry point, then check whether the replacement location retains records for the same batch. The restoration applies only to the current batch and does not automatically declare that other entry points should also be rolled back. If the issue affects one same-named entry point, still locate it by source and adopters; do not use the name to restore neighboring relationships as well.

Restoring the old entry point does not mean deleting the replacement location. Especially when artifact versions have already been recorded at the new location, erasing the new side outright would break the version relationships within the rollback window. After restoration, review both sides together: whether the old entry point is readable again, whether the replacement location retains this batch's records, and whether consumers have returned to an identifiable path. The index can be marked "Old entry point restored, replacement records pending consolidation"; this is not a migration-complete marker.

The old entry point is eligible for removal only when consumer status is clear, the replacement location is usable, the relevant artifact versions can still be found through the index, and rollback is no longer needed. If any condition is missing, retain the old entry point, the replacement location, and the original notes. Removal here applies only to the corresponding index row; it does not constitute a conclusion about the entire `.github/workflows` queue.

There is an explicit minimum for the old entry point being "readable": whoever takes over can find the original location, associated artifact versions, and records from before and after rollback. It does not promise that all historical actions can be repeated in their original way, nor does it interpret retaining the old page as meaning that the old path is still the recommended entry point. This distinction avoids conflating recovery needs with migration recommendations.

## March Addendum

After the rollback replay was completed, the way exit entry point records are read needs to be corrected. The collection policy change point has been inserted into the timeline, so trends before and after that point cannot be compared directly. This change did not expand the migration batch or alter the relationship between the old entry point and the replacement location; it changed how the records are interpreted during recovery.

The recovery page showing a normal status only means that the recovery page has recovered; differences before and after the policy change cannot be attributed to any one entry point. After the recovery page turned green, the first record at the exit entry point still arrived two minutes later. These two minutes must not be recorded as a rollback failure, nor deleted from the records alongside the index. This shows that the recovery page and the exit entry point are not the same signal; trends should be read in segments divided at the policy change point, rather than connecting the values before and after it into one continuous trend.

The rollback replay action for BTCD-005 is complete, but completing the action does not replace migration confirmation for each consumer. It only gives this round of exit actions a result that can be revisited. The current handoff action for BTCD-012 was also completed as part of the maintenance batch; this resolves who takes on this particular action, not long-term maintenance ownership. Index rows whose long-term maintainer has not been confirmed continue to show unknown and are not rewritten because the temporary handoff is complete.

BTCD-010 has completed risk review, so this version retains separate columns for "source" and "adopters." The purpose of this format is to let subsequent checks locate the actual entry point relationships first, then decide whether to consolidate the records; it does not require all same-named pages to migrate to the same location. Notes that cannot be rechecked remain out of date until the actual consumers can fill in the missing relationships.

The first broken link is still recorded at DOC-42. Only when the break lies between the old entry point and the replacement location should you return from there to this index to check the corresponding row; DOC-42 does not hold migration records for build queues or artifact versions. BTCD-005, BTCD-010, and BTCD-012 can be used to find the contexts for rollback, splitting same-named entry points, and temporary handoff, respectively.

## Current Order of Operations

1. Find the index row for the old entry point and verify its connected build queue and artifact versions.
2. Record the replacement location and classify consumers as confirmed, still using the old entry point, or not yet rechecked; separate same-named entry points by source.
3. Switch only confirmed consumers within the rollback window. Retain the old entry point for items not yet rechecked and for possible restoration.
4. When restoration is needed, first restore the usable path for the old entry point, then check whether the replacement location retains artifact records for the same batch.
5. After the recovery page returns to normal, check the first record at the exit entry point separately. If there is a collection policy change, read the timeline in segments.
6. Remove that row's old entry point only after consumer status, artifact versions, the replacement location, and the rollback window all align.

# btcjson Signal Desk Window Closeout Checklist

Before the window ends, check only borrowing through the current entry point, the final output, the return time, and the entry point for withdrawing adj-btcjson. This checklist follows the window practice used at the time: save the failure sample first, then decide whether to issue the final output; other release decisions are outside this checklist.

1. [ ] Enter through `docs/adj-btcjson/release/btcjson-quality-signal-board-pre-window-close-checklist.md`. Do not backfill records from a bypass page with the same name. If the entry point contains `typed error`, keep that text verbatim beside this window's final output.

3. [ ] Write down the return time actually recorded after borrowing began. Use the time for this window, not the expected time for the next round. If a return has happened but no time is recorded, treat it as incomplete.

4. [ ] Check whether `compatibility reader` appears in the materials left at the current entry point. If not, stop here; do not substitute successful samples from elsewhere. The purpose of this stop is to avoid treating output from another path as the conclusion for the current entry point.

Neither `short write` nor a missing `compatibility reader` is a state you can bypass by adding a sentence of explanation. In the former case, preserve the run's state; in the latter, leave the gap. # Shared Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

This page has long served as a quick reference for the team's shared entry point maintenance. The same three questions keep coming up: how much we can say after seeing the storage-index entry point, whether there is a designated person to take over when a candidate path needs to be withdrawn, and when a question counts as resolved. The first two versions left both useful pointers and old criteria that are easy to misread. This version records them separately without erasing the old answers.

**What does having an entry point for storage-index tell us?**

The early short answer was "having an entry point means it has been reviewed." That statement remains in the history, but it can no longer be taken literally. storage-index shows that shared maintenance still has an accessible place to look back at: people can use the records on the page to find the candidate path and confirm that the path does not exist only in someone's verbal recollection. It does not attach the execution records from the offline matrix to the entry point, nor does it assess the candidate version on the reader's behalf.

Two things need to be considered separately here. The entry point itself answers "where to continue looking"; the candidate version's status answers "whether it meets the conditions to proceed to sign-off." The entry point's continued existence does not imply that complete offline records are available; if the entry point cannot be found temporarily, the missing page alone does not establish that the candidate has definitely been withdrawn. The previous version collapsed these two things into "the path has been reviewed," which was precisely where it was most likely to mislead maintainers. Without original execution records, we can only identify the gap; we cannot infer execution results from the existence of an entry point.

**Who do we contact when a candidate path needs to be withdrawn?**

The old draft said "contact the last person who touched the entry point." That was only an ad hoc practice at the time, not a stable ownership mapping. The available material records no fixed name, role, or handoff sequence for withdrawing candidate paths, so editing a page is not grounds for assigning withdrawal responsibility directly to that person. While the candidate path remains visible, retain both the withdrawal request and the entry point itself; that leaves something to cross-reference in later searches, but it does not mean anyone has taken it on.

Withdrawal ownership and issue closure are not the same action, either. Someone finding that an entry point no longer works only indicates that the candidate path needs attention; someone adding the issue to the shared entry point does not establish that withdrawal is complete. If the follow-up question is "who confirmed the withdrawal," and the material contains no original execution record, this page still does not provide a name. The question can remain logged, with the answer left unknown; do not substitute "the last person who touched the entry point" for the missing record.

**When can it be closed?**

"The release module graph is parseable, so it can be closed" is the old criterion and covers only one release-side check. The full statement the team continues to use is: "A candidate version may proceed to sign-off only when all four cumulative chains are closed simultaneously in the offline matrix and the release module graph is parseable." This governs whether a candidate version can proceed to sign-off; it does not automatically mark every question in the shared entry point as complete.

Before closing anything, first confirm what is being closed. Candidate versions are assessed against the conditions for the four cumulative chains and the release module graph; questions about withdrawal ownership that lack original execution records cannot be closed along with them simply because the candidate entry point still exists or the module graph is now parseable. DOC-50 contain similar single-variable rerun notes and can be consulted as related records, but they cannot supply a withdrawal owner for this page or turn one rerun into a complete basis for closure.

# Public Entry Single-Variable Trial Run Log

The initial draft left only a narrow opening for a rerun: use the repository state of module-release as the baseline, without changing the call entry point or replacing the original execution records. At the time, rerunning under the same entry was treated as straightforward: if these three items stayed fixed, the difference could be attributed to the one input that changed. That assumption remains here; it did not say how much actual impact the record could still represent after the old entry was withdrawn.

This review did not create a separate summary. First put the first round's original execution records back in the baseline position, then rerun through the same call entry point. Keep the repository state fixed at module-release and change only one input condition. This is not intended to turn entry maintenance into a complete process; it avoids moving the repository state, entry, and input at the same time and then having no way to tell which one to revisit after a divergence appears.

The record now has three fields:

- Actual impact: write only the parts of this change that can already be matched to the original execution records; do not fold speculation into the result.
- Coordinator: leave this for whoever needs to handle public entry maintenance; the rerun itself has not established more specific ownership.
- Old entry that can be withdrawn: mark this separately. It is not a new baseline condition, but a historical entry outside the rerun that still changes how the results are read.

The rerun ended at the first visible divergence. No third run was used to flatten the records from the first two rounds, and no final conclusion was written from them. Each round remains intact because if only a consolidated result were left later, it would not show whether the divergence appeared after the input changed or whether handling of the old entry shifted the observation point.

The initial draft's wording that "a rerun through the same entry is enough to show the impact" can now only be treated as the working assumption it was at the time. The review added record fields for actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry that can be withdrawn, but did not confirm whether comparison can still be made through the original entry when the old entry is withdrawn. It also did not assign the repository state of module-release as permanent ownership; here it is only the state fixed for this baseline.

Next time, change only whether the old entry is withdrawn. Keep the repository state of module-release, the call entry point, and the original execution records unchanged. If the divergence still appears at the same point, add it to the "Actual impact" field; if the divergence occurs earlier, retain both rounds' original records and do not merge them into one result.

Addendum: if the next round changes only the old entry's status, first leave the original line numbers before and after the divergence side by side. While the coordinator remains unconfirmed, leave that field blank; do not use the state of module-release as a substitute for ownership.
