# Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

Maintaining the public entry point did not become a file ownership reassignment merely because of one follow-up check. The starting point for the discussion remains the chain-state entry point: it has been retained as a common point of contact, while the transition window was proposed to prevent the old entry point from remaining indefinitely on the edge of handoff. Placing both matters in the same review, the draft brought them too close together, making it easy to assume that looking at just one internal location had already produced a complete transition decision.

This addendum retains the original implementation conclusion while clarifying its scope. The current entry point remains in place; the transition window was not approved as a ready-made transition arrangement; and the old entry point must remain revertible. Here, "remain in place" applies only to the public point of contact supported by existing evidence. It does not make commitments about unverified callers, nor does it treat the location of internal code as the public interface itself.

## Two approaches on the review table

**Retain the current chain-state entry point.** This approach keeps existing discussions and follow-up checks anchored at the same starting point. It does not require callers to switch entry points immediately, nor does it require deciding first where the internal implementation should be located. The cost is that the old entry point continues to consume maintenance attention; if a transition really occurs later, "the entry point has already been retained" cannot be used in place of an explanation of the specific path.

**Transition window.** This approach places the transition within a clearly defined handoff arrangement instead of allowing the old and new descriptions to remain side by side indefinitely. Its advantage is that impacts, coordination items, and the rollback point can be handled in the same arrangement. That is also the problem: those elements do not automatically exist merely because the arrangement is called a "transition window." Until the window boundaries are explained by actual evidence, it can only be a candidate approach and cannot be recorded as a completed migration.

This round selects the former as the current arrangement and retains the latter as a position, rather than collapsing the two approaches into an ambiguous middle state. Retaining the entry point does not mean approving long-term dual tracking; deferring the window does not mean rejecting the possibility of opening one later. What the decision rejects is the sequence of stating a transition conclusion first and then looking back for the path and rollback method.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Retain current chain-state entry point] --> C[Continue retaining]
    B[Transition window] --> D[Deferred]
    C --> E[Revertible old entry point]
    F[Actual call path] --> H[Protocol change discussion]
    G[Replayable message] --> H
    J[Targeted Go test] --> H
    H --> I[Internal implementation location]
```

The two lines in the diagram do not mean that all materials must appear in the same form in the same discussion. They record the sequence adopted by the review: first settle the public entry point arrangement within the scope that can already be explained; when a protocol change is involved, start with the actual path, replayable messages, or focused tests, and discuss the internal implementation location afterward. Mixing these two sequences would misstate a collaboration decision as a conclusion about directory structure.

## Points that need correction in the draft

The draft's "retain first" was intended as an implementation constraint, not as a judgment that could end the discussion. It did not sufficiently distinguish among three questions: where existing calls actually arrive, whether there is verifiable support for a protocol change, and whether the implementation layer needs to be reorganized. These often arise together, but new information on any one of them does not automatically answer the other two.

Accordingly, subsequent addenda should not say, "We already looked at `chain state`, so the entry point no longer needs attention." The more accurate reading is: the current public entry point can still serve as a common point of contact; if someone claims that a particular path has changed, they should be able to trace back to that actual call; if someone claims that protocol behavior has changed, a replayable message or targeted Go test should support the local judgment; only afterward should it be discussed whether the implementation location should change accordingly. Any scope not covered by the evidence remains outside the window.

This does not turn the review into a set of formatting requirements. The actual call path answers where the subject under discussion really travels. A replayable message makes it possible to recheck a protocol input under the same conditions. A targeted Go test preserves a follow-up checkpoint for local behavior. The internal implementation location answers how the code should be arranged. Each addresses a different question, and they cannot replace one another merely because their names are similar.

## Wording for actual impact

The direct impact of this round on the existing usage surface is narrow: the current chain-state entry point remains available, unverified paths are not brought into the transition scope by the meeting record, and the old entry point is not removed by this decision. The transition window did not receive implementation status, so it also did not create a new entry point that everyone can be assumed to be following.

These impacts should be read together. Saying only "retain the current entry point" could easily be understood to mean that the old entry point is fixed in place forever; saying only "there is a transition window" could instead be understood to mean that a new entry point is already available for integration. The actual decision lies between those two interpretations: retain the current point of contact, acknowledge that the window is an approach for further discussion, and require the old entry point to remain revertible.

Internal implementation can follow its own reorganization schedule. As long as that reorganization is not connected to a public entry point change by an actual call path, message, or test evidence, it should not be called a protocol transition in this decision. Conversely, a path may need to change without requiring all internal locations to be standardized first. Public entry point maintenance is concerned with points of contact and impact in the collaboration, not with assigning a permanent identity to every implementation file.

## Approval scope

This round approves the scope covered by existing evidence. This limitation works in two directions: verified local content may continue to be maintained on that basis; content that has not been explained cannot be counted as approved merely because it belongs with chain-state or has a similar name. What this leaves is not a blank exemption, but a place for subsequent evidence to attach.

A protocol change must start from an actual call path, a replayable message, or a targeted Go test before the internal implementation location is discussed. The review adopts this wording to prevent a change in public behavior from being inferred directly from a code directory or internal refactoring. If the discussion has only implementation-side observations, the conclusion should remain on the implementation side; only when the evidence explains a particular call and its corresponding behavior may that path be included in the entry point maintenance judgment.

This also explains why the transition window was not approved in this round. A window is not an abstract cleanup action. It means that someone will hand off the entry point relationship along a defined boundary and know where to return if problems arise. Without an explanation of the actual impact, a record that can take ownership of the coordination items, and a rollback point for the old entry point, recording the window early as a transition plan would only hide the gaps until after the handoff.

## Old entry point and rollback

The reason for retaining the old entry point is neither nostalgia nor an assumption that all future calls must pass through it. It is the rollback point in the current arrangement: before the transition has been explained, the old point of contact cannot be removed first and the original relationship inferred afterward from failures or feedback. Revertibility means that a later transition must at least explain which retained entry point the handoff can return to if it fails or if the judgment proves invalid.

This does not expand rollback into a fixed step-by-step procedure. Different paths may require different explanations, and the materials do not provide a unified operation. The current decision leaves only the necessary constraints: the old entry point remains; the transition window was not approved; and no new transition claim may skip discussion of the actual path and verifiable evidence. If only a reason for internal reorganization appears later, the old entry point may remain; if a particular path later has sufficient evidence, the window can be reconsidered for that path.

The reservations should also be archived. The view supporting the transition window is concerned that the old entry point will remain on the public contact surface for too long, until no one takes responsibility for moving the handoff forward; that concern has not been denied. The view supporting continued retention points out that switching early, before the window boundaries, coordination items, and rollback point are clear, would shift the risk to users. This decision does not pretend that either concern has disappeared; instead, it responds to them respectively by retaining the old entry point and deferring the window.

## Coordination record

Coordination is not inferred from a local location such as `blockchain/thresholdstate_test.go`. The file and call name were once used as the starting point for a follow-up check and can help anchor the discussion to an inspectable object; they are not the team's permanent maintenance ownership for the public entry point, nor can they replace coordination details in the handoff.

This record requires three things to be made explicit in any subsequent handoff: which actual impacts have been explained, who will own the coordination items related to the transition window, and where the old entry point will remain revertible. See DOC-52 for the specific transition handoff. This page retains only the reasons this round did not directly approve the window and why the old entry point should nevertheless remain part of the decision.

If subsequent evidence changes any of these items, add a note according to what changed: whether an actual call path was added, whether a replayable message or targeted Go test was added, or whether only the understanding of the internal implementation was updated. The first two categories may expand the entry point scope that can be discussed; the last should still be handled only as implementation-side information. In this way, public entry point maintenance will not be turned by a single local follow-up check into an irreversible overall transition.

# Public Entry Point Switch Handoff Notes

Migration of the public entry point is batched by callers still using the old entry point, not by definition file. `txscript/standard.go` and call names can still serve as starting points for tracing back to script-policy; they cannot replace the consumers listed in the handoff record. The review still did not produce a set of source locations that could be used directly as a migration checklist, so retain the old entry point and record known consumers one by one.

This handoff covers only the switch from the old entry point to the candidate path. A visible definition somewhere does not make the candidate path a replacement for the public entry point. For each batch, first identify the entry point the caller currently uses, then determine whether it can restore its old path on its own. Callers without a restoration action are not included in trial batches. This prevents a problem with the candidate path from becoming a situation where all consumers are unable to roll back at once.

## Handoff Order

First list known consumers, their entry points, and whether they can roll back independently. Here, "roll back independently" means only that the caller can restore its own old path without depending on unfinished coordination across wire, chain, PSBT, or module boundaries. If a consumer has not yet been identified, mark it as pending investigation. Do not include it among migrated consumers or assume it uses the same entry point because another caller's trial succeeded.

```text
Before the switch
Old entry point
  └─ Known consumers

Trial
Candidate path
  └─ One consumer that can roll back independently

Restoration
Old entry point
```

Before the trial, retain the old entry point and record the entry point this consumer currently uses. After connecting it to the candidate path, assess only whether this one consumer can enter and exit the candidate path. Do not use this round to declare that the public entry point for script-policy has been replaced. Other callers continue to use the old entry point, waiting for their own batch records.

## What to Record for Each Batch

Handoffs across wire, chain, PSBT, and module boundaries must include the baseline revision, the failing command, and callerFang Ke-visible differences. The baseline revision is the comparison baseline from before this batch began switching, not a value carried over from another batch. The failing command must be a command that was actually run and failed. If there was no failure, this field may be left blank; do not fill it with a successful run.

For callerFang Ke-visible differences, record the changes the caller actually saw after moving from the old entry point to the candidate path. If it is not yet possible to determine whether a difference belongs to wire, chain, PSBT, or a module boundary, retain the symptoms as seen by the caller rather than rushing to assign them to a layer. This gives the next batch concrete observed differences rather than a guess that has already been interpreted.

The recommended order for filling out a batch record is:

1. Record the consumer's name and its current old entry point;
2. Record this batch's baseline revision;
3. Confirm that the consumer controls the action needed to restore the old path;
4. Connect to the candidate path and record callerFang Ke-visible differences;
5. If it fails, retain the failing command and its direct output, then restore the old path.

The first batch's baseline revision, difference descriptions, and rollback action belong only to the first batch. Subsequent consumers must record their own entry points and differences, even if they appear similar. If a consumer cannot roll back independently, keep it on the old entry point and record the missing restoration action as a handoff issue. Do not automatically mark it as migrated because the previous batch went smoothly.

## Restoration After Failure

If a trial fails, do not remove the old entry point yet. Save the failing command and its direct output, then execute the restoration action already confirmed for that consumer. After restoration, also record the state in which the candidate path was left and whether the caller has already seen any visible differences. Writing only "rolled back" is not enough to distinguish problems caused by the entry point switch from differences in the caller's own integration.

Restoring the old path does not mean this batch can be removed from the handoff table. Keep the failure record under that consumer, and do not expand use of the candidate path. If the failure occurred during a handoff across wire, chain, PSBT, or module boundaries, retain the values captured at the time. Do not overwrite the failing command or difference descriptions with a normal result from a run after restoration.

## Conditions for Proceeding

Consider removing the old entry point only after the consumer list and all batch handoffs have been collected. If any of the following is missing, the status remains migration in progress:

- Known consumers and their respective entry points;
- The action for restoring the old path for each trial participant;
- The baseline revision for the corresponding batch;
- The failing command and its direct output when an actual failure occurred;
- CallerFang Ke-visible differences between the old entry point and the candidate path.

This review adds the batch sequence, record fields, and stopping points for restoration. Fields still missing from the actual runs remain blank. Select the next batch from the known consumer list; do not treat the candidate path's readiness for a trial as completion of the full switch.
